name: Patterned / holographic PEI-family plate (PEI, PEO or PEY)
summary: A cosmetic novelty surface that transfers a rainbow diffraction pattern onto the bottom face of a print. The optical effect comes from microscopic grating ridges — roughly 500-1500 nm spacing — embossed or etched into the coating, not from pigment. The critical caveat is chemical: many plates marketed as 'patterned PEI' are not polyetherimide at all but PEO or PEY films, which top out far lower on temperature and wear out much faster than genuine PEI. Buy for the look, not for versatility.
surface_makeup: Varies by vendor and is frequently mislabelled: either genuine polyetherimide with the diffraction pattern embossed or etched in, or (more often on budget plates) a PEO or PEY film laminated over an adhesion layer on spring steel. Diffraction-grating ridges at roughly 500-1500 nm spacing produce the holographic effect; related 'carbon-fibre-look' PET plates are purely cosmetic film with no actual carbon fibre
manufacturers: generic AliExpress and Amazon plate vendors

preparation: On first use, wipe gently with IPA on a soft lint-free cloth to remove manufacturing residue — gently is the operative word, because the diffraction ridges that create the effect are nanometre-scale and abrade easily. Routine prep is a light IPA wipe before printing; never scrub hard, and never use steel wool or an abrasive pad to 'restore' grip the way you would on smooth PEI, since flattening the ridges destroys the pattern permanently. Keep fingers off the print area and re-run first-layer calibration when swapping from another plate type. Because these coatings are thinner than powder-coated PEI, dial the Z-offset in slightly conservatively on the first print rather than pushing the nozzle in.
cleaning: Routine cleaning is a light 90%+ IPA wipe when cold, using minimal pressure. Avoid acetone and every other aggressive solvent — the general PEI-family caution applies and these films are thinner and more delicate than a powder coat. Avoid metal scrapers entirely. Notably, glue stick is discouraged here for cosmetic rather than functional reasons: it visibly dulls the holographic effect even where it helps release (per 3DBite; unverified independently), so if a material needs a separator, that is usually a sign it belongs on a different plate. For baked-on residue, warm the bed and lift with a plastic scraper rather than cutting cold.
model_removal: Cool and flex, like the rest of the PEI family: let the plate reach room temperature, lift it off the magnet, and flex gently until the part releases. Two differences matter. First, some PEO-based variants are reported by their own vendors not to self-release on cooling, so expect to flex manually more than you would on textured PEI. Second, the coating is a thin film rather than a thick powder coat and is reported to peel or delaminate under aggressive prying (unverified severity), so use a plastic scraper sparingly, at a shallow angle, and never lever against the film. Removing parts hot is the fastest way to ruin one of these plates.
stuck_print_recovery: Work gently and prefer the least mechanical option available. Start with a full cool-down and repeated gentle flexing. Alcohol wicking at the perimeter works as it does on other PEI-family surfaces and puts no mechanical stress on the film. Unwaxed dental floss or thin wire drawn under a corner is the preferred mechanical assist, since it distributes force instead of concentrating it under a blade tip. The freezer trick is reported to work but should be used cautiously given the thinner coating and its adhesive layer; community reports flag the holographic layer lifting or peeling when parts are pried aggressively, so accept a slower recovery rather than risk the surface.

damage_avoidance.item: Steel wool, sandpaper and abrasive pads
damage_avoidance.reason: The restoration trick that works on PEI is fatal here. The holographic effect comes from diffraction ridges at roughly 500-1500 nm spacing; any abrasive flattens them on first contact, and unlike a powder coat there is no fresh layer underneath to expose. Both the pattern and the adhesion consistency go at the same time, permanently.

The general PEI-family caution applies with less margin, because these plates are usually not PEI at all. Vendors use PEI, PEO and PEY interchangeably for demonstrably different polymers, the working layer is a thin film rather than a thermoset coat, and there is an adhesive lamination underneath that solvent reaches quickly at the sheet edges. No manufacturer publishes a chemical-resistance spec for the holographic layer.

damage_avoidance.item: Metal scrapers and levering with any tool
damage_avoidance.reason: Community reports describe the holographic layer lifting or peeling when parts are pried aggressively, though the severity varies between brands and no vendor documents it. Because the film is thin and laminated rather than bonded into a coat, a blade does not merely score it, it starts a peel that keeps running. Use floss or wire under a corner instead.

damage_avoidance.item: Removing parts while the plate is hot
damage_avoidance.reason: The fastest way to ruin one of these plates. Grip is highest at bed temperature and the film has the least mechanical reserve of any surface in this catalogue, so hot removal peels rather than releases. Complicating this, some PEO-based variants are described by their own vendors as not self-releasing on cooling, so expect to flex manually and be patient rather than reaching for heat.

damage_avoidance.item: High-temperature filaments and bed temperatures above roughly 120 degC
damage_avoidance.reason: PEO, PEY and PET plates are commonly quoted at up to 120 degC, and vendor guidance is that ABS, PA and PC belong on PEI or high-temperature plates rather than these. The 120 degC figure is a repeated marketplace number, not a datasheet value, and it varies by vendor, so treat it as soft. Running hot shortens the already brief window in which the pattern stays vivid.

Discouraged here for appearance rather than function: glue visibly dulls the holographic effect even where it improves release (per 3DBite, unverified independently). Since the pattern is the entire reason to own this plate, a material that needs a separator is a signal it belongs on a different surface.

Reported to work, but riskier than on a powder-coated sheet. The stack is a thin film over an adhesive layer over steel, and each of those interfaces has a different contraction rate, so cold-shock adds peel stress exactly where the failure mode already is. Accept a slower recovery with alcohol wicking or floss before reaching for the freezer.

damage_avoidance.item: Soaking, or letting liquid pool at the sheet edges
damage_avoidance.reason: On a laminated film the perimeter is the weak point. Liquid that wicks under an edge attacks the adhesion layer and starts a lift that spreads with every subsequent heat cycle. Wipe with a barely damp cloth rather than washing these plates under a tap.

lifespan_notes: Materially shorter-lived than standard PEI. Community reports put vivid holographic effect at roughly 50-100 print cycles before visible degradation, which is far faster than a powder-coated PEI plate wears. As the diffraction pattern flattens, both the cosmetic effect and adhesion consistency decline together. There is no recoating path — these are replaceable novelty consumables, and they are priced accordingly. Running high-temperature materials, applying glue stick, or scrubbing hard all shorten that window further.

price.notes: Roughly USD 15-30 for 220-310 mm class sheets from third-party AliExpress and Amazon sellers; Creality's PEY/PEI Rainbow magnetic flex plate for K1 Max-class beds falls in the same band (unverified exact figure).

additional_notes: This is a cosmetic category first and a build surface second: it is chosen for the rainbow pattern transferred to a print's first layer, not for adhesion performance or material breadth. Treat the word 'PEI' in these listings with suspicion — PEO and PEY substitutions are common and carry materially different temperature and durability characteristics, and vendors use the three names interchangeably. Neither Bambu Lab nor Prusa Research sells a first-party holographic plate in their reviewed lineups (unverified). Plates are typically magnetic-mount with a single patterned side, the reverse being plain smooth or textured PEI, rather than patterned on both faces.

provenance.conflicts: The central unresolved issue is chemical identity: vendors use 'PEI', 'PEO' and 'PEY' interchangeably for plates that are demonstrably different polymers with different temperature ceilings, and no manufacturer publishes a technical spec for the holographic layer. The roughly 120 degC ceiling is a commonly cited figure for PEO/PEY coatings, not a datasheet value, and it varies by vendor. Self-release behaviour is contradictory: some listings claim clean cool-down release while other PEO variants are explicitly described as not self-releasing. The 50-100 cycle effect-lifespan figure is community anecdote with no controlled testing behind it. Reports of the film peeling under prying vary in severity and may be brand-specific. No first-party Bambu or Prusa product was identified, which is an absence of evidence rather than confirmation none exists. Every specific in this entry should be treated as vendor-dependent.
